title: Process Communication Between Namespaces
markdown:
# Process Communication Between Namespaces

When you run `docker exec -it my-container ip addr show`, Docker is not doing anything exotic — it is finding the network namespace that container's process lives in, and running your command inside that namespace. `kubectl exec` does the same thing one layer up. The command you have been using throughout this module to do exactly that is `ip netns exec`, and this lab is about using it the way an orchestrator does: as a window into otherwise-isolated process worlds, run entirely from the host.

You will build a small two-namespace scenario — `web` and `db`, standing in for two "containers" — and then spend most of the lab not setting things up, but *inspecting* them: comparing what each namespace can see of itself, proving neither can see the other's interfaces directly, and proving that despite that isolation, the host can reach into both and the two can still talk to each other once properly wired.

## The Mental Model: One Host, Many Isolated Worlds

A network namespace gives a process its own private copy of everything network-related — its own interfaces, its own IP addresses, its own routing table, its own ARP cache. A process running inside `web` has absolutely no visibility into `db`'s interfaces, and vice versa — as far as either is concerned, the other namespace simply does not exist.

The host, however, is different. The host created every namespace, so it retains the ability to "step into" any of them on demand with `ip netns exec <name> <command>` — running one specific command inside that namespace's isolated network stack, then returning. This asymmetry — namespaces are blind to each other, but the host (or an orchestrator acting on the host's behalf) can inspect any of them — is exactly the relationship between a container and the Docker daemon, or a pod and the kubelet.

| What | Stands in for |
|------|----------------|
| `web` namespace | A "web" container |
| `db` namespace | A "db" container |
| `veth-web` / `veth-db` | The container's virtual NIC |
| `ip netns exec <ns> <cmd>` | `docker exec <container> <cmd>` / `kubectl exec <pod> -- <cmd>` |

## Part 1: Building Two Isolated Worlds

First, the setup — this should feel familiar from earlier labs in this module. Two namespaces, one veth pair connecting them directly.

```bash
sudo ip netns add web
sudo ip netns add db

sudo ip link add veth-web type veth peer name veth-db
sudo ip link set veth-web netns web
sudo ip link set veth-db netns db

sudo ip netns exec web ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec web ip link set veth-web up
sudo ip netns exec db ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec db ip link set veth-db up

sudo ip netns exec web ip addr add 10.80.0.1/24 dev veth-web
sudo ip netns exec db ip addr add 10.80.0.2/24 dev veth-db
```

At this point you have two namespaces, each with its own address, connected by a single direct veth pair — the simplest possible two-"container" topology. The interesting part starts now.

## Part 2: Looking Into Each World From the Host

Every single command below follows the same shape: `ip netns exec <namespace> <command>`. The `<command>` can be absolutely anything you would run on a normal Linux box — `ip`, `ping`, `cat`, `ps` — the namespace is transparent to the command itself; only the network view it sees changes.

```bash
# Peek into web's network state
sudo ip netns exec web ip addr show
```

This prints `web`'s interfaces exactly as if you had SSH'd into a separate machine and run `ip addr show` there — except you never left the host, and this took milliseconds instead of a login.

```bash
# Peek into db's network state
sudo ip netns exec db ip addr show
```

Compare the two outputs. `web` only ever reports `lo` and `veth-web` — it has no concept of `veth-db` or `db`'s address. This is not a permissions restriction; the interface genuinely does not exist from inside `web`'s namespace. If you ran plain `ip addr show` (no `ip netns exec` prefix) right now, you would get the **host's** interfaces instead — proof that "current namespace" is a property of where the command runs, not something you can discover by asking a namespace what else exists nearby.

```bash
# web's own routing table — has no knowledge of db's internals
sudo ip netns exec web ip route show
```

`web`'s routing table contains exactly one thing: the directly-connected `10.80.0.0/24` route created automatically when you assigned its address. It has no entry mentioning `db` by name, no visibility into `db`'s routing table, nothing — the only thing `web` "knows" about `db` is an IP address on a subnet it happens to share.

**Why it matters**: this is precisely the guarantee a container orchestrator relies on. A compromised or misbehaving container cannot enumerate its neighbors' network configuration just by looking around inside its own namespace — the isolation is structural, enforced by the kernel, not by an access-control list that could be misconfigured.

## Part 3: Isolated Does Not Mean Unreachable

Isolation and connectivity are two different axes. `web` and `db` are fully isolated from each other's *view* of the network, yet they are also directly wired and can reach each other — the same way two Docker containers on the same bridge network are isolated processes that can still `curl` each other by IP.

```bash
sudo ip netns exec web ping -c 3 10.80.0.2
sudo ip netns exec db ping -c 3 10.80.0.1
```

Both succeed in both directions. Neither namespace needed to be told anything about the other beyond an IP address on a shared subnet — connectivity comes from the wiring (the veth pair), not from either side being aware of the other's existence.

## Part 4: The Host's-Eye View

Finally, step back to the host level entirely. While neither `web` nor `db` can see each other, or even know how many other namespaces exist on the machine, the host can enumerate every single one:

```bash
ip netns list
```

This is the same relationship `docker ps` has to your running containers — a flat list, from the one vantage point (the host) that has visibility into everything, while each individual namespace remains blind to its siblings.

## Conclusion

`ip netns exec` is not just a setup tool for wiring namespaces together — it is the general-purpose mechanism for running any command inside an isolated network world, which is exactly what container runtimes build `exec` on top of:

- A namespace sees only its own interfaces, addresses, and routes — never another namespace's, no matter how closely connected they are
- The host (or an orchestrator) can step into any namespace on demand with `ip netns exec`, even though the namespaces cannot see each other
- Isolation of *view* and isolation of *reachability* are independent — two namespaces can be wired together and fully reachable while remaining completely blind to each other's configuration
- `ip netns list` gives the host a flat inventory of every isolated world it has created — the same relationship `docker ps` has to containers

Everything in this module — namespaces, veth pairs, bridges, NAT — are the raw kernel primitives that `dockerd`, `containerd`, and `kubelet` assemble into "containers" and "pods." There is no additional magic layer: a container's network is a namespace, a container's NIC is a veth end, and `docker exec` is `ip netns exec` with a friendlier name.
